Pick idea one: a new-patient lead-generation and appointment-setting service for dental offices. 

You already work as a receptionist in a dental office, giving you an insider edge, immediate access to an avatar, and daily insight into the exact operational pain points competitors ignore. This fits the rule of selling a skill people already pay for. Idea two requires $6,000 in inventory, risking most of your $11,000 savings on a capital-heavy model. Idea three buys a route netting $700 a month, which falls far short of replacing a $3,400 salary within 18 months.

Your first 90 days should follow a strict operational sequence focused on consistent yardage rather than a Hail Mary:

Days 1–30: Build the Offer and Secure Your First Client
Map the exact steps of how front desks mishandle new-patient calls. Package your service around the single compelling point of fixing missed calls and booking appointments. Leverage your industry proximity to sign your first dental office on a performance or monthly retainer model to validate the offer without outside ad spend.

Days 31–60: Document Proof and Refine Delivery
Focus entirely on fulfillment. Gather concrete proof (such as increased booked appointments) because proof beats promise. Use this real-world evidence to build a simple, dedicated landing page highlighting your specific service. 

Days 61–90: Outbound Sales and Volume
Do not buy ads yet. Use high-volume outreach—cold calling and direct messaging dental practice managers—leveraging your insider credibility. Make and keep your promises to secure early case studies. 

Assumptions: Dental offices struggle with lost new-patient revenue due to front-desk bottlenecks, and you can dedicate your 20 weekly side-business hours entirely to direct sales and service delivery. 

Decision Criteria: If you fail to secure even one paying dental client within the first 60 days using your direct industry background, re-evaluate whether your offer solves a painful enough problem before spending money on traffic.
